@@136457399 <h> When Faith Becomes State Power : The Rise of Institutionalised Christian Extremism <p> This paper examines the theological , hermeneutical , and political conditions under which state-sponsored religious extremism has taken root within the executive and military apparatus of the United States . It does so by analysing five interconnected scholarly domains : the biblical doctrine of Herem and its systematic misapplication in contemporary political discourse ; the tradition of Palestinian Liberation Theology as developed by Naim Ateek , Mitri Raheb , Munther Isaac , and Yohanna Katanacho ; the phenomenon of Christian nationalism and its most incisive theological critics ; the comparative political theology of religiously sanctioned violence across the Abrahamic traditions ; and the history and critique of what has variously been termed " Empire theology . " The argument advanced is not that Christianity as a tradition is inherently violent , but that a specific , institutionalised mutation of evangelical Christian nationalism -- one that fuses apocalyptic eschatology with the machinery of the most powerful military state in human history -- constitutes a qualitatively distinct and globally catastrophic form of religious extremism . The voices of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ consequences of Western biblical misuse for generations , are treated not as peripheral commentary but as primary scholarly interlocutors whose insights carry the evidentiary weight of lived experience . <p> Introduction : The Sacralisation of Terror <p> Terrorism , at its core , is the instrumentalisation of violence and fear to achieve political or ideological objectives . It functions by bypassing the traditional boundaries of conflict , transforming the victims of violence into symbolic messages intended to coerce , demoralize , or radicalize the survivors . When such violence is sacralised through religious language , it undergoes a dangerous transformation : the political actor no longer seeks mere earthly victory but claims to execute a divine mandate , rendering the act of destruction immune to human ethical or legal constraints . <p> The phenomenon of " Christian terrorism , " as explored in this paper , is not an inherent expression of the Christian tradition but a qualitative mutation -- a systematic subversion of the Gospel 's message of peace and reconciliation . It represents a radical misuse of sacred texts and religious emotions , where the " Prince of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . This ideology exploits the deep-seated spiritual longings of the faithful -- their desire for moral clarity and their eschatological hope -- and channels them toward the " ulterior purposes " of state expansion , geopolitical hegemony , and the maintenance of imperial power . <p> By fusing apocalyptic eschatology with the machinery of the modern state , this institutionalized extremism creates what can be termed a " liturgy of the void . " It justifies the obliteration of the " other " by framing contemporary geopolitical rivals as ancient ontological enemies , such as Amalek . In doing so , it betrays the very faith it claims to defend , replacing the ethical rigor of the Just War tradition with a reckless zeal for catastrophe . The following analysis examines this crisis , treating the voices of those who live under the shadow of this theology -- most notably Palestinian Christians -- as the primary witnesses to the global danger posed by the marriage of cross and sword . <p> The Hermeneutics of Holy War <p> The Hebrew word herem -- rendered variously as " the ban , " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " -- occupies one of the most contested positions in the entire corpus of biblical scholarship . Derived from a root connoting separation or consecration , herem in its oldest textual strata designated an object , person , or community irrevocably given over to the divine -- either as a gift to the sanctuary or , more troublingly , as material subject to total obliteration . The logic is precise and brutal : that which is placed under the herem can not be redeemed by human agency . It belongs entirely to God , and its destruction is an act of worship . <p> The passages most relevant to contemporary misuse are Deuteronomy 7:1-2 , which commands the extermination of seven Canaanite nations ; Deuteronomy 25:17-19 , which mandates the " blotting out " of Amalek ; and 1 Samuel 15 , in which Saul 's failure to execute King Agag in fulfilment of the herem against the Amalekites becomes the precipitating cause of his divine rejection . These texts , embedded within the specific literary and theological contexts of Deuteronomistic History , have generated centuries of interpretive controversy . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the maximalist view , which takes the herem narratives as more or less historically reliable accounts of Israelite practice ; the minimalist view , which treats them as late literary constructions with little historical basis ; and the canonical-hermeneutical view , which insists that whatever their historical provenance , their significance must be read within the progressive arc of biblical revelation . <p> The canonical-hermeneutical position is the most theologically sophisticated and the most consequential for the present analysis . Scholars such as Christopher Wright and Walter Brueggemann have argued at length that the herem narratives function within the canon as specific , unrepeatable episodes in a covenantal drama that reaches its telos in the New Testament . Wright , in The God I Do n't Understand ( 2008 ) , acknowledges the profound moral difficulty of these texts while insisting that they can not be read as timeless warrants for violent action . The conquest narratives , he argues , were geographically and historically bounded , typologically fulfilled in Christ 's defeat of cosmic evil , and explicitly superseded by the New Testament 's redefinition of the " enemy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The critical point for this paper is not merely exegetical . It is the observation that a rigorous engagement with the scholarly literature on herem reveals a near-universal consensus among biblical scholars that the concept can not be legitimately transferred to modern geopolitical conflicts . The invocation of Amalek or the Canaanite ban as a template for 21st-century military action represents not an application of biblical theology but its deliberate inversion -- the conscription of sacred text into the service of political violence by stripping it of its literary , historical , and canonical context . <p> The Amalek Archetype in Contemporary Political Discourse <p> The concern is not with ancient history alone . In October 2023 , Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu invoked 1 Samuel 15:3 -- " Now go , attack the Amalekites and totally destroy all that belongs to them " -- in an address to Israeli soldiers mobilising for operations in Gaza . The invocation was not incidental or metaphorical ; it was a direct citation of the herem command applied to a contemporary population . Commentators across the political spectrum , including Orthodox Jewish scholars @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Amalek identification has a long and dangerous history in Jewish messianic nationalism , where it has been used to designate contemporary enemies as inheritors of Amalekite ontological wickedness -- a status that places them outside the ordinary protections of moral law . <p> Within the American context , the Amalek archetype has migrated into the discourse of Christian Zionism and dominionist Christianity with considerable velocity . Figures associated with the New Apostolic Reformation -- a loosely organised network of charismatic leaders who exercise significant influence over sections of the evangelical Republican base -- have deployed a comparable logic of categorical divine enmity towards Iran , the Palestinians , and Islam broadly . The theological mechanism is consistent : an ancient narrative of total warfare is abstracted from its historical and canonical context , given a new set of contemporary referents , and used to generate a divine mandate for violence that is , by definition , immune to diplomatic or ethical objection . God has ordained it . To question it is to question God . <p> Palestinian theologian Naim Ateek , writing in Justice and Only Justice ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) , identified these hermeneutical move decades ago and gave it a precise critical vocabulary . He termed it " biblical land-grabbing " -- the practice of selectively appropriating texts to legitimate political projects while systematically ignoring the textual and canonical context that would subvert such projects . Ateek 's critique is not primarily negative . He proposes a " liberation hermeneutic " in which the primary criterion for biblical interpretation is whether a given reading promotes or obstructs justice for the oppressed . On this criterion , the application of the herem to contemporary populations fails absolutely : it transforms the God revealed in Christ as the protector of the vulnerable into a tribal deity commissioning ethnic cleansing . <p> The Purim Inversion : Esther as Warrant for Pre-emptive War <p> A related hermeneutical distortion involves the Book of Esther and its annual commemoration in Purim . In its canonical form , the narrative is one of survival : a persecuted minority , threatened with genocide by a court official named Haman , is delivered through the courage of Esther and the wisdom of Mordecai . The theological resonance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reversal of imperial power , and the importance of human moral agency within providential history . <p> In the hands of certain American evangelical and Christian Zionist commentators , however , this narrative has been systematically inverted . Iran , a largely Persian nation , is identified with the ancient Persian antagonist Haman ; the modern state of Israel and its American backers are cast as Esther and Mordecai ; and the narrative logic of Purim is used to justify not defensive survival but offensive pre-emption . The argument runs : as Haman plotted the destruction of the Jews , so Iran now plots the destruction of Israel ; as Esther acted before the blow fell , so must the United States and Israel act before Iran acquires the capacity to strike . The story of survival is repurposed as a mandate for aggression . <p> This inversion is theologically illiterate in multiple respects . It also ignores the profound ambiguity of the Esther narrative 's own ending , in which the formerly threatened Jews become the agents of considerable violence -- a dynamic that many Jewish scholars read not as a celebration but as a troubling commentary on the cyclical nature of vengeance . <p> Mitri Raheb , in Faith in the Face of Empire ( 2014 ) , offers the decisive critical framework here . Raheb argues that the recurring pattern of Christian and Jewish engagement with biblical narrative in imperial contexts is one of self-identification with the dominant power . Empires , he observes , always need a sacred narrative that casts their violence as divine necessity and their expansion as providential mission . The Purim inversion performs precisely this function : it places the world 's most heavily armed nation in the position of the vulnerable minority , thereby transforming offensive war into existential self-defence and clothing imperial aggression in the theological garments of Jewish survival . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Liberation Theology emerged as a recognisable scholarly and pastoral movement in the late 1980s , shaped by the confluence of two distinct intellectual currents : The Latin American liberation theology that had been transforming Catholic and Protestant thought since the 1960s , and the specific experience of Palestinian Christians living under Israeli military occupation . The movement is not a monolith . Its leading figures -- Naim Ateek , Mitri Raheb , Munther Isaac , and Yohanna Katanacho -- represent different ecclesiastical traditions , different methodological approaches , and different emphases within a shared commitment to reading the Bible from the underside of political power . <p> The methodological cornerstone is what liberation theologians call the " hermeneutical privilege of the poor " -- the claim , grounded in both the prophetic tradition and the New Testament , that those who suffer structural injustice occupy an epistemically privileged position for discerning the political and ethical dimensions of biblical texts . This is not a claim to infallibility or to the irrelevance of academic biblical scholarship . It is rather a claim that the lived experience of oppression -- including the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that are supposed to be one 's inheritance -- generates interpretive insights that are unavailable to those who read the Bible from positions of comfort and power . <p> Naim Ateek , an Anglican priest and the founder of Sabeel Ecumenical Liberation Theology Centre in Jerusalem , is the movement 's most systematic theologian . His landmark work , Justice and Only Justice ( 1989 ) , written in the immediate aftermath of the First Intifada , established the core problematic : how does a Palestinian Christian read a Bible that has been used , generation after generation , to justify the dispossession of their people ? Ateek 's answer is a christological hermeneutic : Jesus Christ , as the fullest revelation of God 's character and intention , is the primary criterion by which all other biblical material must be assessed . Texts that , in their apparent plain sense , advocate violence , ethnic exclusion , or the divine right of one people to the land at the expense of another must be read through the corrective lens of Christ 's teaching , particularly the Sermon on the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is at pains to insist that this is not a rejection of the Hebrew Bible but a christological fulfilment of its deepest trajectory . <p> Mitri Raheb , a Lutheran pastor based in Bethlehem and the founder of Dar al-Kalima University , brings a distinctive political-theological lens to the tradition . His most sustained theoretical contribution is the concept of " Empire theology " -- a pattern of religious thought that Raheb traces across multiple historical periods , in which religious institutions and narratives are co-opted by dominant powers to legitimate their hegemony . In Faith in the Face of Empire ( 2014 ) , Raheb argues that the geography of the Eastern Mediterranean has made Palestine a perpetual site of imperial contest , from the Babylonian and Roman empires through the Crusader kingdoms to the British Mandate and American hegemony . In each case , the dominant theological narrative has served the interests of the power that controls the land . <p> Raheb 's analysis is notable for its refusal of simple binaries . He is equally critical of all forms of Empire theology , whether they emanate from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that might be tempted to mirror the exclusivist nationalism they oppose . His vision of a Palestinian church that witnesses to the God of life against all powers of death is rooted in a political theology of the cross -- the insistence that God is most fully revealed not in the spectacular violence of conquest but in the suffering of the crucified , who is identified with all those crushed by imperial power . <p> In The Politics of Hope ( 2011 ) , Raheb extends this analysis to a critique of Christian Zionism as a specifically American theological export that serves American geopolitical interests while presenting itself as fidelity to biblical prophecy . Christian Zionism , he argues , is not a neutral reading of eschatological texts ; it is a theological product of 19th-century Protestant dispensationalism that has been weaponised in the 20th and 21st centuries to provide sacred sanction for American involvement in the Middle East . Its effect on Palestinian Christians has been devastating : they find themselves erased from the theological imagination of their Western co-religionists , who recognise Jewish and Muslim actors in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ communities that have maintained a continuous presence in the Holy Land for two millennia . <p> Munther Isaac , an evangelical theologian and pastor at Christmas Lutheran Church in Bethlehem , represents a younger generation of Palestinian liberation theologians whose work engages more directly with Western evangelical Christianity on its own hermeneutical terrain . His book The Other Side of the Wall ( 2020 ) is written explicitly for a Western evangelical audience and employs the internal logic of evangelical biblical scholarship to challenge the Christian Zionist appropriation of land theology . Isaac argues that the New Testament does not simply continue the land promises of the Hebrew Bible but radically transforms and universalises them : the " land " that Christ promises to his followers is not a specific territorial possession but the whole renewed earth , and the " people of God " is not an ethnically defined nation but a community constituted by faith in Christ across all ethnic and national lines . <p> Isaac 's 2023 Christmas sermon , delivered from Bethlehem under the shadow of the Gaza conflict and widely circulated under the title " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ theological significance that transcends its homiletical occasion . Its central claim -- that God in Christ is found not in the triumphant violence of the powerful but under the rubble with the crushed and the dying -- is not merely pastoral consolation . It is a political-theological argument : The God revealed in the Incarnation can not be the God who sanctions the bombing of hospitals and the destruction of civilian infrastructure , because the Incarnate One is specifically identified with those who suffer such destruction . To invoke Christ as the inspiration for such violence is not Christianity but its systematic negation . <p> Yohanna Katanacho , an Arab-Israeli theologian and academic , brings a rigorous engagement with New Testament scholarship to the tradition 's treatment of land , temple , and the community of the Spirit . In The Land of Christ ( 2013 ) , Katanacho traces the New Testament 's progressive redefinition of the sacred geography of the Hebrew Bible . The land of Israel , he argues , is fulfilled in Christ 's body and in the community of those who are " in Christ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nations and ethnicities . On this reading , the " Temple theology " that drives segments of the Christian Zionist and Jewish messianic nationalist agenda is not a fulfilment of prophecy but a regression to pre-Christian categories that implicitly denies the sufficiency of Christ 's atoning work . <p> Christian Nationalism and Its Theological Critics <p> The academic study of Christian nationalism has matured considerably in the past decade , producing a literature that distinguishes carefully between phenomena that popular discourse often conflates . The sociologists Andrew Whitehead and Samuel Perry , in Taking America Back for God ( 2020 ) , offer the most widely cited typological framework , distinguishing between " accommodators , " who accept a general cultural Christianity in public life ; " resisters , " who oppose any fusion of Christian identity with national identity ; and two intermediate positions . Their empirical work demonstrates that Christian nationalist ideology @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to be a Christian nation , with political institutions reflecting Christian values as defined by conservative evangelicalism -- is a significant predictor of authoritarian attitudes , racial resentment , and support for political violence . <p> It is important , however , to distinguish Christian nationalism from conservative Christianity , evangelical Christianity , or even theologically orthodox Christianity as such . The theological critics of Christian nationalism are not liberal secularists uncomfortable with religious presence in public life ; they are , in many cases , orthodox Christians who believe that Christian nationalism represents a profound theological error -- a category confusion between the Kingdom of God and the Kingdom of the United States that corrupts both Christianity and democracy . <p> Among the most cogent of these critics is the Baptist theologian Russell Moore , whose departure from the Southern Baptist Convention was in part precipitated by the failure of that institution 's leadership to maintain the distinction between Christian identity and Republican political allegiance . The prophetic function of the church -- speaking truth to power , advocating for the poor , maintaining independence from the state -- is fatally compromised when the church becomes the ideological apparatus of a particular political programme . <p> The New Apostolic Reformation and Dominionist Theology <p> A distinct and more theologically radical strand of Christian nationalism is represented by the New Apostolic Reformation ( NAR ) and the broader dominionist or " Seven Mountains " movement . Where traditional Christian nationalism seeks to preserve or restore a culturally Christian America , dominionism seeks the active transformation of all sectors of society -- government , media , education , business , family , arts , and religion -- under explicit Christian ( understood as Spirit-filled evangelical ) authority . The theological basis is a particular reading of the " Cultural Mandate " of Genesis 1:28 and the eschatological expectation of a victorious church that will establish God 's kingdom on earth before or in preparation for Christ 's return . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the years surrounding the Trump presidency , when figures associated with the movement occupied prominent advisory and pastoral roles in relation to the White House and the military . The theology of the " anointed " leader -- the belief that God raises up specific individuals to exercise divine authority over nations in a way that transcends ordinary accountability -- is a central NAR concept with obvious and dangerous political implications . When military commanders describe their orders as " biblically sanctioned " or characterise their president as " anointed by Jesus , " they are deploying NAR theology , whether or not they would use that terminology . <p> The theological critique of dominionism from within orthodox Christianity is well-developed . The Anabaptist tradition makes a related argument with greater radicality : the very possession of coercive political power by the church is a betrayal of the cruciform pattern of Christ 's life and mission . <p> Institutionalisation : The Pentagon as Prayer Room <p> The institutionalisation of specifically Christian nationalist and dominionist theology within the United States military is a development that has been carefully documented by the Military Religious Freedom Foundation ( MRFF ) , founded by Mikey Weinstein , a former Air Force officer and White House Fellow . The MRFF 's case files represent a systematic record of complaints from service members -- the majority of them Christian -- who report coercion , discrimination , and command-level proselytisation . The picture that emerges is not one of individual bad actors but of a structural pattern in which evangelical Christianity has been woven into the fabric of military culture at senior levels . <p> The significance of this for the present analysis is not merely constitutional . The separation of church and state , while important @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ issue is theological and ethical : when the officials who control the world 's most destructive military apparatus believe themselves to be acting under divine mandate , the ordinary constraints of strategic rationality , legal obligation , and humanitarian ethics are potentially dissolved . The Just War tradition -- itself a product of Christian theological reflection , developed by Augustine and systematised by Aquinas -- requires that warfare be conducted for a just cause , by legitimate authority , with right intention , as a last resort , with a reasonable chance of success , and with proportionality in the means employed . None of these criteria apply , or can be made to apply , when the objective is understood as the fulfilment of divine prophecy . A war designed to precipitate the apocalypse can not be assessed for proportionality . A strike authorised by the Lord of Hosts does not require the exhaustion of diplomatic alternatives . <p> A definitive instance of this theological institutionalization occurred in April 2026 , following the military engagement designated ' Operation Epic Fury ' in Iran . " <p> A comparative approach to religiously sanctioned violence across Judaism , Christianity , and Islam reveals both structural similarities and important differences that are frequently obscured in political discourse . All three traditions contain texts and interpretive traditions that , under specific conditions , have been used to legitimate violence ; all three also contain powerful counter-traditions that subordinate or transform those violent elements . The question is not which tradition is inherently more violent -- a question that is unanswerable and methodologically @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of each tradition to become dominant , and what resources each tradition possesses for self-critique and restraint . <p> In the Jewish tradition , the concept of herem , discussed above , represents the most extreme form of divinely mandated violence . However , the dominant trajectory of post-biblical Jewish legal thought ( halakha ) radically curtailed the practical applicability of herem , eventually rendering it inoperative in the absence of prophetic authority . The Talmudic rabbis were acutely aware that the mechanisms of sacred violence , if left operative , posed an existential threat to the community , and their legal creativity in rendering them non-applicable reflects a sophisticated theological instinct for self-preservation . Contemporary Jewish religious extremism -- exemplified by settler ideology and the writings of figures such as Meir Kahane -- represents not a recovery of ancient practice but a radical innovation that breaks with the dominant tradition of rabbinic caution . <p> In the Islamic tradition , the concept of jihad has been subjected to analogous processes of interpretation and constraint . Classical jurisprudence distinguished carefully between the " greater jihad " ( the internal struggle @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ armed conflict ) , and the conditions under which the lesser jihad was licit were tightly circumscribed : it required legitimate authority , just cause , proportionality , and the protection of non-combatants . The violent extremism of groups such as al-Qaeda and the Islamic State represents , as many Muslim scholars have argued at length , a radical departure from the mainstream of Islamic jurisprudence -- a departure enabled by the collapse of traditional scholarly authority , the trauma of colonialism , and the deliberate misreading of contextually specific Quranic passages . <p> The parallel with Christian extremism is instructive and important . Just as Islamic terrorism represents a distortion of Islamic tradition enabled by specific historical and political conditions , the institutionalised Christian extremism under analysis here represents a distortion of Christian tradition enabled by specific conditions : the fusion of dispensationalist eschatology with American exceptionalism , the erosion of mainline Protestant institutional authority , the rise of charismatic parachurch networks , and the capture of sections of the evangelical movement by a specific partisan political project . In both cases , the tradition itself contains the resources @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be effectively mobilised . <p> Asymmetric Capacity and the Meaning of " Arch " <p> One dimension in which the comparative analysis does yield a genuine asymmetric finding concerns not the intensity of theological motivation but the scale of destructive capacity available to different actors . This is a structural observation , not a moral one , and it requires careful articulation . <p> Non-state terrorist actors -- whether motivated by Islamic , Jewish , or Christian ideology -- are constrained by their lack of access to industrial military capacity . Their violence , however horrifying in its immediate effects , is necessarily limited in scale . State actors are not subject to this constraint , and when religious extremism achieves institutionalised influence within a state apparatus , the potential scale of violence expands catastrophically . This is not a new observation . The religiously motivated massacres of the colonial period -- the extermination of indigenous populations in the Americas , the partition violence in South Asia , the genocides of the 20th century -- were all instances in which state capacity was deployed in contexts shaped by religious ideology @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Christian nationalist eschatology with American military capacity is the addition of a further variable : the eschatological desire for catastrophe . A conventional state actor , however aggressive , is typically deterred by the prospect of mutual destruction . An actor who believes that mass destruction fulfils divine prophecy and hastens the return of Christ is not deterred by catastrophe -- they are motivated by it . This removes the fundamental logic of deterrence and transforms the traditional calculus of military decision-making in ways that have not been adequately theorised within either political science or strategic studies . <p> Just War , Jihad , and the Limits of Theological Constraint <p> The Abrahamic traditions have each developed sophisticated theological frameworks for constraining and regulating violence . The Christian Just War tradition , rooted in Augustine 's response to the challenge of governing a Christian empire , seeks to permit violence in extremis while surrounding it with moral conditions that prevent its unlimited expansion . The Islamic jurisprudence of jihad , as noted , imposes analogous conditions through a different legal mechanism . Jewish halakha 's treatment of milchemet reshut @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> These traditions are not equivalent -- they differ in their institutional mechanisms , their theological presuppositions , and their historical track records . But they share a fundamental orientation : the recognition that violence , even when sometimes necessary , is a moral evil that requires justification , constraint , and accountability . What is at stake in the contemporary institutionalisation of Christian extremism within the American state is precisely the abandonment of this orientation . The Just War tradition is not discarded ; it is simply rendered irrelevant by the claim of direct divine mandate . When God has ordained the destruction , the criteria of proportionality , last resort , and discrimination do not apply . <p> This is the theological core of the present paper 's central argument . The danger is not simply that certain individuals hold extreme views , but that a theological framework has been institutionalised within a state apparatus that renders the ordinary constraints on violence inoperative . The " arch " quality of this terrorism -- its primary , structural , and institutionalised character -- lies precisely in this : @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a theological system that makes violence obligatory and restraint sinful . <p> Empire Theology -- History , Analysis , and the Path of Resistance <p> The concept of " Empire theology " -- the systematic co-optation of religious thought and institutional structures to legitimate imperial power -- did not originate with Mitri Raheb , though his treatment of it is among the most analytically precise . The pattern is visible from the moment that Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire under Constantine , a development that many church historians regard as the most significant turning point in Christian history -- significant not because it was obviously beneficial , but because it was deeply ambiguous . <p> The Constantinian settlement created what the theologian John Howard Yoder called " Christendom " -- a social arrangement in which the boundaries of the church and the boundaries of society are coextensive , and in which the church therefore trades its prophetic independence for a share in social power . The consequences for Christian theology were far-reaching . The theology of the cross -- the insistence that God is most fully @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ power -- was progressively displaced by a theology of triumph in which the church 's power is treated as evidence of divine favour . The Sermon on the Mount 's ethic of non-retaliation and enemy-love was hedged about with qualifications until it applied , if at all , only to private life -- the public sphere of politics and warfare being governed by a different , more accommodating ethic . <p> Empire theology , in this genealogy , is not an aberration but the dominant form of Western Christianity for most of its history . The Crusades , the conquest of the Americas , the blessing of colonial violence by European churches , the German Protestant support for National Socialism -- these are not anomalies ; they are iterations of a recurring pattern in which the institutional church identifies its interests with those of the dominant power and constructs theological justifications for that identification . What distinguishes the current moment is the specific theological content ( apocalyptic dispensationalism rather than civilisational Christianity ) , the specific political context ( American global hegemony in a period of perceived decline ) , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ than established state churches ) . <p> The theological underpinning of contemporary American Empire theology is the doctrine of American exceptionalism -- the belief , with deep Puritan roots , that the United States has a unique , divinely appointed role in human history . John Winthrop 's 1630 sermon aboard the Arbella , with its image of a " city upon a hill , " established the foundational trope : America as a providential experiment , its success or failure a matter of cosmic significance . This is not merely a political myth ; it is a theological claim , and it has been extraordinarily durable . <p> In its 21st-century dispensationalist mutation , American exceptionalism is fused with a specific eschatological timeline in which America 's role is to support the state of Israel until the final battle that will usher in Christ 's return . This fusion is theologically extraordinary . It requires the identification of a modern secular state with the biblical Israel of prophecy , the identification of a contemporary superpower with the divinely appointed instrument of providential history , and the subordination of all @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ prophetic timeline . The result is a theological system that is , in its internal logic , totalitarian : there is no sphere of life , no human relationship , no international obligation that is not potentially overridden by the demands of eschatological fulfilment . <p> The political consequences are considerable . If the destruction of Iran is a prophetic requirement , then diplomacy is not merely imprudent but sinful -- a human attempt to frustrate divine purpose . If the dispossession of Palestinians is prophetically mandated , then advocacy for their rights is not merely politically mistaken but theologically treasonous . This is the logic of Empire theology in its most extreme contemporary form , and it is not the theology of a fringe . It is , as polling data consistently demonstrates , a significant strand of mainstream American evangelical Christianity . <p> The Counter-Tradition : A Theology of the Crucified <p> The resources for resistance to Empire theology are not to be found primarily in secular liberalism or progressive politics , though these may be important allies . They are found within the Christian tradition itself , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the cross over the crown , the priority of the suffering servant over the conquering king . <p> Palestinian Liberation Theology is one powerful expression of this counter-tradition . Its insistence that God is found under the rubble rather than above the clouds , that Christ is the Palestinian child in the wreckage rather than the American general giving the order , that the Bible is a resource for the liberation of the oppressed rather than a blueprint for the hegemony of the powerful -- these claims are not additions to Christian theology from outside . They are recoveries of dimensions of the tradition that Empire theology systematically suppresses . <p> The monastic traditions , the Anabaptist and Mennonite communities , the Catholic Worker movement , the liberation theologians of Latin America -- all represent moments in which the church has refused the Constantinian bargain and maintained its identity as a community defined by the cross rather than the sword . The significance of Palestinian Liberation Theology within this broader counter-tradition is that it is produced not from comfortable European or North American contexts but from a situation of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that the broader argument is concerned with . Ateek , Raheb , Isaac , and Katanacho are not theorists of Empire theology ; they are its victims , and their witness carries a moral and theological authority that is unavailable to those who analyse the phenomenon from positions of safety . <p> The Kairos Palestine document of 2009 , signed by a broad coalition of Palestinian Christian leaders , represents the most significant institutional expression of Palestinian Liberation Theology 's political-theological witness . Its title deliberately echoes the Kairos Document produced by South African theologians in 1985 , which challenged the apartheid regime 's theological justifications for racial separation . The Palestinian Kairos document addresses Western Christians directly , calling them to recognise that their theological and financial support for Israeli state policies that violate international law constitutes a complicity that they must repent of and resist . <p> The document 's theological framework is precisely that which this paper has been analysing . It insists that the Bible can not be read as a political document justifying the dispossession of one people for the benefit of another ; that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ exclusivism ; that love of neighbour , as defined by Christ , can not be limited to those who share one 's ethnicity or political allegiance ; and that the Christian vocation in the present moment is not to hasten the apocalypse but to bear witness to the possibility of a different kind of future -- one defined by justice , reconciliation , and the dignity of all human beings as bearers of the divine image . <p> The reception of the Kairos document in Western Christianity has been uneven . Where it has been engaged seriously , it has generated productive theological conversation . Where it has been dismissed -- and it has been dismissed , sometimes viciously , by Christian Zionist organisations that characterise it as anti-Semitic -- the dismissal itself is theologically revealing . To characterise an appeal for justice grounded in the New Testament 's most basic ethical principles as anti-Semitic is to perform , in miniature , precisely the hermeneutical move that the entire paper has been analysing : the subordination of the universal ethical imperatives of the Gospel to a specific political programme . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The Theological Stakes <p> This paper has argued , across five interconnected domains of analysis , that what might be called the institutionalisation of Christian extremism within the American state represents a development of profound theological and political significance . The argument is not that Christianity is inherently violent , or that all Christian engagement with politics is dangerous , or that the United States has no legitimate security interests . The argument is more specific and more alarming : that a particular mutant form of Christian theology -- one that fuses apocalyptic dispensationalism with American exceptionalism , misapplies the concept of herem to contemporary geopolitical conflicts , deploys " Empire theology " to sacralise state violence , and has achieved significant institutional influence within the executive and military apparatus of the world 's most powerful state -- constitutes an existential danger that demands urgent theological , political , and ethical response . <p> The voices of Palestinian Christian theologians are central to this analysis for reasons that go beyond their intrinsic scholarly merit , though their work is of genuine scholarly distinction . They are central because they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ generations , under the consequences of the theological distortions under analysis . When Naim Ateek argues that the use of herem rhetoric to justify contemporary violence is a " scriptural assassination , " he speaks not from theoretical discomfort but from the experience of a people whose humanity has been systematically denied by the very texts that are supposed to witness to the God who creates all human beings in the divine image . When Mitri Raheb insists that Empire theology always needs an enemy , he speaks from a geography that has been the site of imperial contest , and theological justification for that contest , for millennia . When Munther Isaac places Christ under the rubble , he speaks from a city , Bethlehem , in a land where the rubble is not metaphorical . <p> The comparative analysis across the Abrahamic traditions reveals that the structural conditions for religiously sanctioned violence are not unique to any single tradition , and that each tradition possesses within itself the resources for self-critique and restraint . The specific danger of the present moment lies not in the novelty of religious @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to it and in the erosion of the theological , legal , and institutional constraints that might otherwise check it . The Just War tradition , the Geneva Conventions , the separation of church and state , the prophetic independence of the church -- all of these are simultaneously under theological attack from within and political attack from without . <p> The response that this analysis demands is not primarily political ; though political action is necessary . It is primarily theological : the recovery , articulation , and proclamation of a Christianity that centres the crucified Christ rather than the conquering king ; that reads the Bible as a witness to the God of universal love rather than a blueprint for ethnic hegemony ; that understands the church 's vocation as the bearing of prophetic witness against all forms of imperial violence rather than the provision of theological cover for it . The Palestinian theologians whose work has informed this analysis have been performing precisely this recovery under conditions of acute suffering . Their work is not peripheral to Western Christian theology ; it is , in the present @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ liturgy of the void -- the prayer that invokes the name of God to consecrate the obliteration of those made in God 's image -- is not the last word of the Christian tradition . The last word , as Munther Isaac preached from Bethlehem amidst the ruins , is still the Word made flesh , dwelling under the rubble , refusing to be extinguished . That theological insistence is not naivety ; it is the most politically consequential claim the Christian tradition possesses , and its recovery is the only adequate theological response to the darkness here analysed . For two adversaries locked in intense and seemingly irreversible hostility since the 1979 Islamic Revolution , the very articulation of such an ambition marks a significant shift . <p> Yet the fragility of the moment is evident . Confusion over the opening and closing of the Strait of Hormuz ; arguments over rival blockades ; US President Donald Trump 's optimism Tuesday ( April 21 ) about a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Iran 's infrastructure if Tehran does n't agree ; and the questions very late into this evening over Iranian participation underline the deep mistrust that continues to shadow the talks . If even preliminary coordination remains so contested , the path to a comprehensive settlement will be arduous . <p> The Trump administration , however , appears committed to thinking big . Vice President J D Vance , expected to leave for a second round of talks in Pakistan soon , has publicly framed the negotiations not as incremental diplomacy but as the quest for a " grand bargain " -- an effort to secure a decisive , system-shaping agreement . The objective is expansive : a comprehensive settlement that trades limits on Iran 's nuclear programme and regional posture for full economic normalisation and reintegration into the global system . <p> This ambition departs sharply from the logic of the 2015 nuclear deal , which was deliberately narrow and technocratic . That agreement sought to cap Iran 's nuclear capabilities but did not address the broader sources of geopolitical conflict between Washington and Tehran , or the interests of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at broadening the settlement . <p> In its essence , the proposed bargain is sweeping . Iran would accept stringent and verifiable constraints on its nuclear programme , potentially including a rollback of enrichment levels , tighter inspection regimes , and limits on stockpiles of highly enriched uranium . More consequentially , Tehran would be expected to recalibrate its regional strategy -- reducing support for non-state armed groups and scaling back its influence across theatres such as Gaza , Iraq , Lebanon , Syria , and Yemen . <p> In return , the United States would move towards dismantling its long-standing and massive sanctions architecture against Iran . This would involve lifting both primary and secondary sanctions , unfreezing Iranian financial assets , and facilitating Tehran 's return to global energy markets and financial networks . The end goal is not merely arms control , but a broader economic and political normalisation . <p> Recent reports suggest that both sides are exploring steps that will allow each to claim early gains while preserving leverage for subsequent stages . This , of course , is easier said than done . Powerful @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ proposed grand bargain . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> Internal divisions in both Washington and Tehran help generate mixed signals , weaken negotiating credibility , and undermine the entire process . Any movement towards a grand bargain is likely to be in clearly defined stages . <p> The most plausible pathway begins with a political understanding -- a broad memorandum outlining principles of de-escalation , mutual recognition , and the desired end-state . This would then be followed by detailed technical negotiations on nuclear verification , sanctions relief , and regional security , with carefully calibrated sequencing . <p> Even here , the challenges are formidable . Verification of nuclear commitments , though complex , falls within the competence of established international mechanisms . Far more difficult is the question of regional behaviour . Measuring and enforcing limits on influence exercised through non-state actors presents a conceptual and operational challenge that diplomacy has rarely resolved successfully . <p> Sequencing remains another major obstacle . Iran will demand credible and front-loaded sanctions relief to justify concessions ; the United States will insist on demonstrable compliance before relinquishing economic leverage @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of reciprocal steps , with built-in safeguards against backsliding . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> Despite all the challenges , the logic of a grand bargain persists . After decades of coercion , confrontation , and failed incrementalism , both sides are confronting the limits of their current strategies . Although the obstacles are substantial , and the risks of failure high , the fact that Washington and Tehran may sit down for another round of talks is a cause for modest optimism . <p> ( C. Raja Mohan is a contributing editor on international affairs for The Indian Express )

" This proposal appears pragmatic on the surface , but at its core it is an expansion of the powers of private security companies to bypass the role of the state and transform into an independent force of social control , operating by the logic of profit rather than the logic of law , independent judiciary , and democratic accountability . <p> Point Twenty demands " resistance to the pervasive intolerance of religious belief . " This point does not stem from a genuine defense of freedom of belief . It is an opportunistic deployment of religious discourse to build an ideological alliance with conservative and religious currents that are most susceptible to mobilization behind war projects @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ alliance with religious institutions to lend violence a sacred character , and this is what this point seeks under the cover of " freedom of faith . " <p> Point Twenty-One is the most revealing of the deep ideological dimension , when it declares that " some cultures have produced vital advances while others remain dysfunctional and regressive . " This sentence is not a passing cultural opinion . It is the theoretical foundation of civilizational colonial racism that justifies domination , occupation , and the killing of peoples under the cover of " rational management of civilization . " <p> This logic does not differ fundamentally from the " white man 's burden " that justified colonialism in previous centuries , and it is being reproduced today in the language of algorithms and big data . What makes it more dangerous than its predecessor is that it requires no visible colonial forces . A database and a targeting algorithm suffice . <p> Trumpism as a System , Not a Person <p> The common mistake is to reduce Trumpism to the person of Donald Trump . Trumpism is a comprehensive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hostility toward immigrants and minorities . At its core , it is an expression of the crisis of capitalism when it can no longer reproduce the liberal illusion for its audience , so it resorts to aggressive nationalist discourse to divert attention from the real class contradictions . What the Palantir manifesto does is link digital monopoly capital to this project and supply it with the technological tools needed to transform it from electoral political discourse into an actual system of control . <p> The documented cooperation between Palantir and immigration authorities and security agencies in tracking and deporting migrants is a practical model of this alliance . Technology here is not used to serve " security " in any neutral sense . It is used to implement repressive and racist policies with high operational efficiency . The digital tool makes repression faster , more precise , and less in need of public justification . <p> Digital Feudalism and Its Fascist Phase <p> As I have previously argued in my analyses of digital capitalism , we are living through the advanced phase of digital feudalism , in which large corporations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ just as feudal lords once monopolized land and controlled peasants . What the Palantir manifesto reveals is that this digital feudalism is now entering its fascist phase , the phase in which capital no longer contents itself with silent economic exploitation but moves toward explicit political and ideological mobilization and control to protect its system from any threat . <p> Under digital capitalism , it is no longer only traditional manual and intellectual workers who are victims of exploitation . Every user produces daily data that is converted into raw material for the production of surplus value without compensation . <p> Digital serfs work within systems they do not own and are subject to rules over which they have no real influence . What the manifesto adds to this picture is militarization : these same exploitative systems are now directed toward framing the human mind , waging wars , suppressing dissent , forcing deportations , and managing systems of security control . <p> Algorithms of Death <p> The manifesto can not be read in isolation from what is happening in contemporary wars . Documented reports have revealed that Palantir has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ targeting databases that are actually used in military operations . This is not a theoretical possibility . It is a documented daily practice : algorithms that convert human lives into data points , and data points into military targets . <p> In Palestine , journalistic and investigative reports have documented the use of artificial intelligence systems to build targeting lists that resulted in massacres against civilians in Gaza . In Venezuela , Iran , and other countries that Washington classifies as " threats , " surveillance and data systems are used to support militarism , aggression , and wars that violate international law . <p> What the company calls a " smart targeting system " is in practice a machine for managing killing with industrial efficiency . Killing no longer requires a responsible human decision . It requires an algorithm , sufficient data , and a green light from an apparatus that is subject to no democratic accountability . This is the field application of what the manifesto calls " real-time decision-making capacity , " where kill decisions are made instantaneously within closed technical systems . <p> Most importantly in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be separated from the discourse that justifies classifying entire communities as backward or threatening . The crime does not begin with the bomb . It begins with the classification . When entire communities are defined as a threat , the killing and targeting of civilians becomes " security management " rather than a crime whose perpetrators must be held accountable . <p> The Illusion of Technological Neutrality , Self-Surveillance and Digital Repression as Tools of Control <p> The danger of the model Palantir is building does not lie solely in its direct military applications . More dangerous still is what can be described as the " surveillance society , " when control becomes internal rather than external . When an individual knows they are being watched at every moment and feels that every digital interaction is being recorded and analyzed , they begin to impose surveillance on themselves . <p> They modify their speech , avoid sensitive subjects , distance themselves from radical dissenting ideas . This voluntary self-surveillance restricts and weakens leftist and progressive movements and labor organizations from within , without the need for arrests or direct restrictions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of human behavior " as a condition for security is in reality a call to build a comprehensive system for disrupting collective political action before it emerges . Predicting protest behavior and dismantling it before it becomes an organized movement is the dream that security services have long pursued , and Palantir 's technology is moving closer to realizing it . <p> Among the most prominent ideological mechanisms of the manifesto is its reliance on closed deterministic logic . " There will be no technological neutrality , " " the question is not whether AI weapons will be built , " " democracies can not rely on moral discourse alone . " This approach aims to convert political choices into inescapable natural facts and to eliminate any questioning of the nature of the existing system from the sphere of legitimate debate . It is the same approach used by neoliberals when they declared in the 1990s that " capitalism is the end of history . " Now the same logic returns in a security formulation : there is no choice but digital militarization . <p> This determinism is not a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ emptying politics of its content . When you are convinced there is no alternative , you stop searching for one . And that is the primary goal behind this language . <p> The Leftist Alternative : The Question of Ownership and Collective Control <p> The Palantir manifesto is not merely a document from a tech company announcing its positions . It is a loud alarm bell that progressive forces must hear clearly : the battle over the future of technology is no longer lurking backstage . It has stepped into the open , announcing itself without shame . Those who delay in grasping this shift delay their entry into the most decisive arena of struggle in this century . <p> The fundamental question is not how technology is used . It is who owns it and who determines its objectives . Technology will not become a tool of liberation as long as it remains in the hands of digital monopolies allied with projects of the right , war , and repression . Any serious discussion must begin from the necessity of collective societal ownership of digital infrastructure , and from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ represents the interests of working masses rather than monopolistic elites . <p> This requires leftist , progressive , and human rights forces to engage with the arena of technology in full seriousness as an important field of class struggle . Producing intellectual critique , however important , is not enough without building actual technological alternatives through coordination and joint work via digital internationals : social platforms free from monopoly , restriction , and repression ; search tools that respect the privacy of all users ; artificial intelligence systems managed in a democratic and transparent manner ; and other digital applications . These are not recreational projects for the future . They are an urgent strategic necessity for any serious liberatory project . <p> Necessary Addition : Technological Disarmament as a Prerequisite <p> Building alternatives alone is not sufficient unless paired with an organized campaign to strip these monopolies of their technological weapons . It should be noted here that Palantir is not an exceptional case or an anomaly in the technological landscape . It is the most explicit and bold expression of what many other companies practice with greater silence @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ focus in this analysis is that it revealed what others are accustomed to concealing , not that it differs from them in substance . The system is one ; the only exception is the degree of frankness . <p> Just as the historical labor movements struggled to disarm capital in factories and farms , today an equivalent struggle is necessary to wrest lethal algorithms , targeting systems , and mass surveillance from the grip of these companies collectively . <p> This struggle takes multiple forms : boycotting their services , exposing their secret contracts with governments , prosecuting their executives before international courts on charges of complicity in war crimes , and pressuring public institutions to sever their relationships with these companies . Every government contract with this system is direct financing of the killing and deportation machine . Stopping this financial flow is the first line of confrontation . <p> This path can not be completed without working simultaneously at both the domestic legislative and international levels . At the domestic level , pressure must be applied to enact strict laws requiring security technology companies to maintain full transparency @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ artificial intelligence systems in military targeting outside any independent judicial oversight , and compelling these companies to submit to the same accountability standards to which public institutions are subject . <p> At the international level , work must be done to subject these companies to international human rights conventions , particularly the Geneva Conventions prohibiting the indiscriminate targeting of civilians , the United Nations charter on the protection of personal data , and the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights . A company that builds targeting databases in war zones can not be permitted to operate outside this legal framework , and if it does , the governments that contract with it bear shared criminal responsibility . This is not a luxury reformist demand . It is the minimum required by the humanity of law in confrontation with the inhumanity of the algorithm . <p> Second Addition : Exposing the Labor Silence at the Heart of the Manifesto <p> What is striking in the Palantir manifesto , indeed what is deeply suspicious , is that it does not mention a single word about workers , about unions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . In a document that speaks of the " engineering elite , " " moral duty , " and " backward cultures , " there is no place for the manual and intellectual workers who build these algorithms , operate them , and live under the weight of the same surveillance . <p> This silence is not incidental . It is an implicit admission that the fascist technological project can not face the workers ' question , because workers alone , if they organize themselves , are capable of stopping the lines of death production entirely . A general strike in Silicon Valley , or even in Palantir 's own offices , is this project 's nightmare . Supporting technology workers ' unions and linking their struggle to a global struggle is therefore an act of resistance of the first order . <p> This technological struggle can not be separated from the popular struggle on the ground . Technology is a supporting tool for the struggle , not a substitute for it . Real power remains in political , labor , and popular organization , in social movements , in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ whether in wars , at borders , or in workers ' neighborhoods surveilled by algorithms that require no one 's permission . <p> Conclusion : Digital Fascism by Its True Name <p> The Palantir manifesto reveals clearly that we face a new form of fascism , not only in the narrow historical sense , but in its essential meaning : the alliance of monopoly capital with aggressive national political power and the deployment of violence , repression , and civilizational hierarchy to protect this alliance from any popular threat . The only difference is that the tools of this fascism today are algorithms , big data , and artificial intelligence , and this is what makes it more airtight and more difficult to resist than what preceded it . <p> When Alexander Karp finishes writing his philosophical manifesto in his elegant office , the algorithms his company built continue their work of identifying targets , tracking migrants at borders , building databases of dissidents around the world , and supporting the machinery of militarism and repression across the globe . Philosophy and crime are two faces of the same coin @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ passes inevitably and substantially through the struggle to liberate technology from this aggressive class alliance . This is not a technical question or an abstract ethical question . It is a political question through and through , and part of a historical struggle over who holds control over the future and human consciousness : the monopolistic minority allied with projects of killing and repression , or the working masses who must impose their authority over the tools that shape their lives and their destiny . <p> Max Weber ( 1864-1920 ) was a prominent German sociologist who developed influential theories on rationality and authority . They are not mere figureheads but active in creating and influencing the public understanding of world events . <p> 3 ) Universal values : intellectuals must apply the same standards of justice universally , avoiding the comfortable narratives of ideology . Universality means taking a risk in order to go beyond the easy certainties provided us by our background , language , nationality , which so often shield us from the reality of others . It also means looking for and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it comes to such matters as foreign and social policy . <p> So , in the end , it is the intellectual as a representative figure that matters . The independent intellectual is among the few remaining personalities equipped to resist and to fight the stereotyping and consequent death of genuinely living things . If the thinker does not relate himself to the value of truth in political struggle , he can not responsibly cope with the whole of live experience <p> Western intellectuals have much to learn from Edward Said 's approach in the face of today 's complex geopolitical reality and its wars . ' <p> Although Trump 's abrasive diplomatic style and given the onset of the Iran War Carney depiction of the world order crisis was interpreted by the media and elsewhere as a global dimension that stretched beyond the fracturing of Atlanticist unity . As well this show of disunity in the West was viewed in many foreign capitals as far preferable to sheepish support for Trump 's posture of ultimatum or annihilation . Yet Carney is ambiguous about whether his message is signaling a rupture of western domination @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more rearrangement of the regional deck chairs in a European version of an inevitable Titanic-type disaster . <p> Supposing that a rupture of world order has occurred , what kind of modifications , if any , are likely to emerge ? Carney fails to make clear , perhaps even to himself , that his concerns are limited and directed exclusively at the non-geographic ethnic groupings encompassed by the Atlanticist Alliance that has led the West since the end of World War II . Its core is the NATO membership of Europe and North America , but its writ extends to the breakaway British colonies of Australia and New Zealand , and more problematically and less civilizationally even to Russia and possibly Turkey . This dominant grouping is an entirely Western grouping of countries mostly committed to constitutional democracy and market-oriented economies , but also by less overtly acknowledged features as white ethnicity and the primacy of Christianity . Carney indirectly probably unintentionally clarified his sense of rupture by a surprising initial endorsement of the American aggression that gave rise to the Iran War , making clear that it was not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rupture , but his concerns were directed at the internal fragmenting of Atlanticism . This perspective was not entirely new , reinforcing my thesis that the present world crisis is about more than oil , Zionism , Iran , Western unity , and even Trump . <p> If so , the question of rupture v. transition needs to be rephased in relation to the global system of interacting states , regions , and civilizations . And not in the manner of Carney , which involves a rearrangement of the components forming the Western civilizational nexus . <p> Carney 's advocated response to rupture was a split in Atlanticism between what he referred to as the ' middle powers ' without specification , but seemingly composed only of Atlanticist states , acting as a balancing offset to American intra-Atlanticist preeminence . It was again not clear whether this was intended by Carney as a reaction to Trump 's approach to Atlanticism or something deeper and more structural . In some unacknowledged way Carney 's March 2026 ' Special Address ' at Davos can be set off against Marco Rubio reaffirmation of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Munich Security Conference with a reassuring emphasis on the continuing vitality of the NATO alliance . <p> Samuel Huntington 's ' clash of civilizations ' argument ( of the West against the rest ) as set forth shortly after the collapse of the Soviet Union was in its way a different image of ' rupture ' than that of Carney . Yet I would classify such a regional development , radical as it might be , as a rupture internal to Western dominance of a hierarchical world order that goes back at least as far as European colonialism that originated modern international relations at the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 . The inclusion of Israel in the civilizational West is of course something new and different from the end of the geographical West . <p> Or if considering the world as a whole , as an altered form of dominance superseding the earlier forms , as epitomized by US aspirations to be ' a global state ' with limited sovereignty and overt territorial claims . This confusion of world and region also is illustrated by referring to both 20th century @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ' regional or European wars . ' These epic wars only felt entitled to use the word world because the region dominated the world , and they are best understood as Western rather than European because the US played a pivotal role in restabilizing Western dominance . <p> George W Bush , back in 2002 , more than two decades ago in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks triumphantly recognized this orientation toward civilizational governance in his cover letter introducing a crucial official document , The National Security Strategy of the United States of America , in these triumphal words : <p> " The great struggles of the twentieth century between liberty and totalitarianism ended with a decisive victory for the forces of freedom -- and a single sustainable model for national success : freedom , democracy , and free enterprise ... We will extend the peace by encouraging free and open societies on every continent . " <p> This model of world order was an explicit recipe for regime-changing interventions throughout the Global South in the early aftermath of the Cold War when the US was behaving like ' @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of democratic , market-oriented development to the Global South under the questionable guardianship of the US in collaboration with the Atlanticist coalition . <p> Obviously , Bush did not envision the spectacular rise of China as challenging the historical triumphalism implicit in these ' end of history ' claims that the US and its satellite liberal democracies had all the answers when it came to national governance , economic development , and global leadership . <p> Bush is oddly relevant for a second reason . His advocacy of and insistence upon the 2003 armed intervention in Iraq was partly publicly justified by seeking to destroy Iraq 's supposed nuclear weapons program and partly as a democracy-promotion project to replace the autocratic regime of Saddam Hussein with a West-leaning rebuilt state supposedly committed to upholding the human rights of its population . <p> This packaging of the Iraq War of 2003 as a ' war of choice ' anticipating the Iran War in basing its primary justification on pursuing national interests through foreign policy without adhering to the constraints of international law . Approaching war as a matter of choice throws @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ refusal of the US even to pretend compliance with international law when it blocked the pursuit of national strategic interests . <p> A telling example of this contempt for international law concerns nuclear weapons . Reading the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty it would seem a forward-looking win/win arrangement for both nuclear and non-nuclear states . The non-nuclear states pledged to give up their nuclear option while the nuclear states agreed to seek good faith negotiations aiming at reaching an agreement among nuclear weapons states to embark upon a secure nuclear disarmament process . The reality of the NPT has turned out differently , to be a procedure by which the dominant nuclear states maintained their geopolitical hegemony while guarding the gate to the nuclear club admitting only selected newcomers . Israel from one point of view , and North Korea from another are the main gatekeeping failures of a purely hegemonic approach to nuclear legitimacy . At the same time , these governments in the West felt entitled to wage unlawful preventive wars to turn back states accused or suspected of ' going nuclear ' or even alleged to convert their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that created the capability to acquire the weaponry on short notice should national security interests so required . We should all ponder if Israel and the United States would have attacked Iran if it indeed possessed a retaliatory nuclear capability . <p> The non-nuclear states apparently accustomed to their subordinate status , maintained over the decades a sullen silence , partially broken to the annoyance of the Western nuclear powers by binding themselves to a Treaty of Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons ( 2021 , as of end of 2025 , 95 signatories , 74 ratifications ) . Iran is alleged by Israel and the US to have become a threshold nuclear state . Even if this were true would it be an unreasonable response to constant threats and destabilizing acts designed to undermine its political independence . Additionally , Iran has been attacked without engendering any condemnation from the international community , either at the UN or elsewhere . Criticism of this second attack on Iran with a single year came mainly from dissident voices in civil society or governments plausibly concerned with the destabilizing impacts of launching an aggressive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> When questioned about this discrepancy between NPT and US behavior , national security insiders retort is along the lines of an admission that ' Article VI ' ( the nuclear disarmament obligations ) has served the country well as ' a useful fiction ' or words to this effect . This confirms the role of international law in US national security policy as a useful tool to criticize adversaries , while at the same time exempting itself and shielding allies from unwanted compliance commitments . In the 2020s these double standards were displayed when the US led the effort to criminalize the 2022 Russian attack on Ukraine while shielding all efforts to criminalize Israeli genocide in Gaza , demeaning and refusing to respect several one-sided judgments of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court that were critical of Israel 's policies and leaders . <p> The pressure to focus all advocacy and activism on averting the geopolitical and humanitarian disasters that are unquestionably imminent in the nuclear age is fully understandable . The gravity and plausibility of present apocalyptic scenarios are undeniable and are currently @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ escalation in Iran and Iran 's resolute resistance even if it means collective martyrdom for the people of the country is a dangerous encounter that could produce a major war disastrous for both parties and the wider systemic wellbeing of the entire planet . <p> Despite the darkness of the hour , I will conclude by offering some brief reflections on ' the day after ' whether this turns out to be a charred landscape of devastation in a country of over 90 million now terrified Iranians or somehow manages deescalation that gives the Iranian people and its neighbors an occasion for a deep sigh of relief . I am aware that there are diverse views about how best to end the Iran War . This somewhat simplistic either/or path that I am hesitatingly endorsing envisions an ending of the war in either catastrophe or peaceful resolution in what I believe most clearly poses the choices facing leaders in the United States and Iran . <p> My first observation along these lines reinforces the earlier point that the world order crisis of our time is systemic , and not only @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ minimum the gradual decline of Western multi-dimensional dominance . This suggest that we need to assess Carney 's rupture/transition reality from a global perspective , and not one implicitly devoted to safeguarding Western geopolitical priorities . <p> In a conceptual shorthand we should also for our own good have the humility to learn from China , and appreciate the peace , justice , development , and ecological benefits of their basic win/win approach to international relations . China has managed to extend its reach to 150 countries that have enjoyed the mutual benefits of infrastructural developments and economic relation without significant encroachment on their political independence and territorial sovereignty . This contrasts with the Western political and economic projections of power over rather than power with other sovereign states in which the status quo is protected , however corrupt , and development is often corrupted , exploitative of native labor , and ecologically harmful . The Chinese approach has a proven record of promoting win/win policies premised on mutual benefits . The restriction must be clearly provided by law , pursue a legitimate aim , and be strictly necessary and proportionate . The state must also identify the precise nature of the alleged threat in an individualised manner and demonstrate a direct and immediate connection between the expression and that threat . <p> Accordingly , general references to the sensitivity or political nature of information are insufficient to remove journalists ' protections , particularly when the publication concerns matters of public interest . <p> This case raises additional concern in light of Decree-Law No. 13 of 2026 on securing and protecting the supreme interests of military entities , which Kuwaiti authorities presented as a tool to safeguard those interests . However , the decree establishes an overly broad framework that imposes secrecy on information and data related to military affairs , prohibits their publication or circulation , and imposes severe criminal penalties , including imprisonment for several years in some cases . <p> Such measures risk criminalising investigative @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ security and military issues .
